name: Functional map of right human hippocampus (v1.0)
description: The hippocampus displays a complex organization and function that is perturbed in many neuropathologies. Histological work revealed a complex arrangement of subfields along the medial–lateral and the ventral–dorsal dimension, which contrasts with the anterior–posterior functional differentiation. The variety of maps has raised the need for an integrative multimodal view. We applied connectivity-based parcellation to 1) intrinsic connectivity 2) task-based connectivity, and 3) structural covariance, as complementary windows into structural and functional differentiation of the right hippocampus. Strikingly, while functional properties (i.e., intrinsic and task-based) revealed similar partitions dominated by an anterior– posterior organization, structural covariance exhibited a hybrid pattern reflecting both functional and cytoarchitectonic subdivision. Capitalizing on the consistency of functional parcellations, we defined robust functional maps at different levels of partitions, which are openly available for the scientific community. Our functional maps demonstrated a head– body and tail partition, subdivided along the anterior–posterior and medial–lateral axis.
new_in_this_version: This dataset version contains the functional map of the right hippocampus. The data of the functional map for the left hippocampus can be found here: [Plachti et. al (2019)](https://doi.org/10.25493/H9X7-6KS)
projects: Multimodal Parcellations and Extensive Behavioral Profiling Tackling the Hippocampus Gradient
publications:
Plachti, A., Eickhoff, S. B., Hoffstaedter, F., Patil, K. R., Laird, A. R., Fox, P. T., Amunts, K., & Genon, S. (2019). Multimodal Parcellations and Extensive Behavioral Profiling Tackling the Hippocampus Gradient. Cerebral Cortex, 29(11), 4595–4612. https://doi.org/10.1093/cercor/bhy336

name: Trans-synaptic signaling and rhythmogenesis in the hippocampus (v1)
description: The CA2 region of the hippocampus has recently emerged as a central structure for social memory processing. Here, in vivo recordings from anesthetized animals have been used to assess the dynamics of neuronal signaling in the CA2 and CA3 hippocampal area. In vivo experiments from NLG3R451C knock-in mice, NLG3 knock-out mice and littermate controls have unveiled a selective impairment of spike-related slow wave activity in the CA2 area and a significant reduction in oscillatory activity in the theta and gamma frequencies range in both CA2 and CA3 regions of the hippocampus. Since transgenic mice are widely used as non-syndromic animal models of Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASDs), data obtained in our experiments can be used by researchers interested in modeling brain activity underlying these neurodevelopmental disorders.
keywords: In vivo electrophysiology in anesthetized animals

name: Probabilistic cytoarchitectonic map of CA3 (Hippocampus) (v13.2)
description: This dataset contains the distinct probabilistic cytoarchitectonic map of CA3 (Hippocampus) in the individual, single subject template of the MNI Colin 27 reference space. As part of the Julich-Brain cytoarchitectonic atlas, the area was identified using classical histological criteria and quantitative cytoarchitectonic analysis on cell-body-stained histological sections of 10 human postmortem brains obtained from the body donor program of the University of Düsseldorf. The results of the cytoarchitectonic analysis were then mapped to the reference space, where each voxel was assigned the probability to belong to CA3 (Hippocampus). The probability map of CA3 (Hippocampus) is provided in NifTi format for each hemisphere in the reference space. The Julich-Brain atlas relies on a modular, flexible and adaptive framework containing workflows to create the probabilistic brain maps for these structures. Note that methodological improvements and updated probability estimates for new brain structures may in some cases lead to measurable but negligible deviations of existing probability maps, as compared to earlier released datasets.
new_in_this_version:
Due to methodological improvements and integration of new brain structures this probability map version has small deviations compared to it's earlier released version. Available coordinate spaces:
+ MNI ICBM 152 (2009c Nonlinear Asymmetric)
+ Colin 27 (1998, cropped)

The most probable delineation of this area is derived from the calculation of a maximum probability map that incorporates all released versions of brain structures at the same point in time. This probability map version was used in the release(s) of the following maximum probability maps::

name: Remapping of place cells in the CA1 area of the hippocampus (v1)
description: This dataset provides data from more than 8000 CA1 excitatory cells in mouse CA1, using a transgenic mouse line Thy1-GCaMP6s with two-photon calcium imaging in freely behaving mice with miniaturized microscopes. A total of 7 mice are included. Five of the mice underwent  an experiment in which they freely foraged open field arenas of different colours (arena A and B), in a three-step paradigm of A-B-A meant to induce global remapping of CA1 place cells. Three of the mice underwent an experiment where they foraged arena A, being exposed to an object within the arena in a four-step paradigm of Empty-Object-Object moved-Empty, meant to show if cells in CA1 respond in relation to the introduced object. Only one mouse underwent both experiments. The mice were foraging for cookies on an 80x80 cm square enclosure, where box A and B had different colours and distal cues, and were located in different parts of the same room. The object introduced was a high-contrast duplo tower approximately 7x7x27 cm of size, unclimbable to the mice. Tracking was performed with an overstage camera and poses extracted using DeepLabCut. Calcium signals, motion correction and ROI detection was performed using suite2p. The data provides both high anatomical precision and high cell yields in freely behaving mice that might be of general interest.
new_in_this_version:
This is version 1 of this dataset. It describes 7 subjects observed via the OpenMini2P mobile two-photon miniscope system [(Zong et al., 2022)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2022.02.017).
For each subject, 1 or more sessions containing 1 or more recordings are included. Each recording consists of a x264 encoded video file monitoring animal position and behaviour within an open arena, and 1 or more tif images recording calcium activity within the subject’s brain.

name: Layer-specific excitatory and inhibitory neuronal maps of hippocampus (v1.1)
description: The aim of this work is to reconstruct the 3D organization of neurons in a left hippocampus from sub-cellular resolution images obtained by a custom-made dual view inverted light sheet fluorescence microscope. The left hippocampus of a 99-year old woman, not affected by Alzheimer’s disease, nor hypertension, but presenting a cognitive decline, obtained from the University of Tours was analyzed. The sample was cut into 72 slices of 500 um thickness before imaging. Each slice was cleared with the SWITCH/TDE method and stained with NeuN (all neurons) and GAD67 (inhibitory neurons). Imaging was performed at a resolution of 1.1 x 1.1 x 3.8 μm³.
new_in_this_version: In the version v1.1 of the dataset "Layer-specific excitatory and inhibitory neuronal maps of hippocampus" the author list is modified compared to the version v1.0. Following contributors have been added to this dataset: Luca Pesce, Vladislav Gavryusev, Annunziatina Laurino & Marina Scardigli
techniques: dual-view inverted selective plane illumination microscopy

name: Density measurements of different receptors for CA2 (Hippocampus) [human] (v2)
description: This dataset contains the densities (in fmol/mg protein) of receptors for classical neurotransmitters in CA2 (Hippocampus) obtained by means of quantitative _in vitro_ autoradiography. The receptor densities are visualized as _fingerprints_ (**fp**), which provide the mean density and standard deviation for each of the analyzed receptor types, averaged across samples. Information on the used tissue samples and corresponding subjects, as well as analyzed receptors accompanies the provided dataset.
new_in_this_version: This version includes the density measurements (**fp**) of Area CA2 for 14 receptor types for the classical neurotransmitters glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine, noradrenalin/norepinephrine, serotonin, and dopamine.

description: This dataset contains cytoarchitectonic delineations of area HATA (Hippocampus) in the BigBrain dataset [Amunts et al. 2013]. The delineations were created after identification of the area in the histological, cell-stained sections based on the cytoarchitectonic criteria. Mappings of the HATA are available on every 15th to 60th section in both hemispheres. They were then transformed to the sections of the 3D reconstructed BigBrain space using the transformations used in Amunts et al. 2013, which were provided by Claude Lepage (McGill).

name: Human Hippocampus scanned by Phase Contrast X-ray Tomography (v1.0)
description: The data has been recorded by X-ray phase contrast tomography, as reported in [Eckermann et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2113835118). It comprises the reconstructed density of hippocampal tissue volume covering a part of the dentate gyrus with 8mm cross section and two binary segmentation masks, for the nuclei of granular neurons and for the vasculature, respectively. The data is from unstained PFA-fixed, dehydrated and paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue, and has been recorded at 0.65µm voxel size at the PETRAIII storage ring in a parallel undulator beam (GINIX/P10 beamline). The data is part of a published study investigating the changes in the cytoarchitecture occurring in Alzheimer’s disease. The data can be used to quantify the short range order of neurons and density in the granular layer, as well as the size an shapes of neuronal nuclei, as well as the spatial relationship between dentate gyrus and the associated vasculature. The dataset can also be used to validate and to improve segmentation methods.

This is the 1. version of this dataset.

name: Absolute number of three populations of interneurons and GABAergic synapses in the human hippocampus (v1.0)
description:
Here we used unbiased stereological methods in combination with light and electron microscopic anatomical investigations in the human hippocampus.
Firstly, we estimated the density and total number of three major GABAergic cell groups in all layers of the human hippocampus of 3 subjects: We examined the inhibitory parvalbumin (PV)-expressing neurons, the somatostatin (SOM)-positive inhibitory neurons and the calretinin (CR)-positive neurons.
Secondly, we used 3-dimensional electron microscopy to determine the total number of
GABAergic boutons and synapses in the different layers of the human hippocampus, and we also quantified those originating from PV-positive cells.
These data describe densities and absolute numbers of GABAergic cells, boutons, and synapses in different sublayers and regions of the human hippocampus. These data will be essential for modeling inhibitory circuits in the human hippocampus.

name: Deep texture features for surface-based characterization of fiber architecture in the human hippocampus (v1)
description:
This dataset contains deep texture features characterizing architectonic patterns of the pyramidal layer in the hippocampal cornu Ammonis region and the subicular complex, as captured by three-dimensional polarized light imaging (3D-PLI).
The 3D-PLI measurements were obtained from 547 individual brain sections of the right hippocampus of an 87-year-old male. Texture features were extracted from 3D-PLI images using a width-reduced ResNet-50 encoder trained on a 3D-Context Contrastive Learning (CL-3D) objective. The features were aggregated along the full depth of the pyramidal layer and transformed into an unfolded coordinate space using HippUnfold. In addition, we provide projections of the feature vectors onto 52 principal components with largest explained variance. These components reflect the general regional organization and reveal an expected functional rostro-caudal heterogeneity of the pyramidal layer.
By transferring features to an unfolded coordinate system using HippUnfold, the data are placed in a canonical reference space, enabling comparisons with other unfolded datasets. Moreover, we provide unfolded surfaces for both the MNI ICBM 152 Nonlinear Asymmetric 2009c and the BigBrain histological space, allowing access to the features within these volumetric reference spaces as well.
new_in_this_version:
This is version 1 of this dataset, containing texture features extracted from 3D-PLI images of a single hippocampus, unfolded using HippUnfold.

Unfolded surfaces are provided for feature access in the following coordinate spaces:
+ Subject space (pli3d)
+ BigBrain histological space (bbhist)
+ MNI ICBM 152 Nonlinear Asymmetric 2009c template (MNI152NLin2009cAsym)

name: Fiber structures of a human hippocampus based on joint DMRI, 3D-PLI, and TPFM acquisitions (v1)
description: The collected datasets provide real multimodal, multiscale structural connectivity insights into the human hippocampus. One post mortem hippocampus was scanned with Anatomical and Diffusion MRI (dMRI) [[Beaujoin et al., 2018] (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29387938)], 3D Polarized Light Imaging (3D-PLI) [[Zeineh et al., 2017] (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/?term=Cerebral+Cortex+27%2C+1779-1794)], and Two-Photon Fluorescence Microscopy (TPFM) [[Costantini et al., 2017] (https://www.osapublishing.org/abstract.cfm?uri=BRAIN-2017-BrW4B.5)], rendering joint tissue imaging possible. MRI scanning was performed with a 11.7 T Preclinical MRI system (gradients: 760 mT/m, slew rate: 9500 T/m/s) yielding T1-w and T2-w maps at 200 µm and dMRI-based maps at 300 µm resolution. During tissue sectioning (60 µm thickness) blockface (en-face) images were acquired from the surface of the frozen brain block, serving as reference for data integration/co-alignment. 530 brain sections were scanned with 3D-PLI. HPC-based image analysis provided transmittance, retardation, and fiber orientation maps at 1.3 µm in-plane resolution. TPFM was finally applied to selected brain sections utilizing autofluorescence properties of the fibrous tissue which appears after PBS washing (MAGIC protocol). The TPFM measurements provide a resolution of 0.44 µm x 0.44 µm x 1 µm.

name: Electrophysiological recordings from entorhinal cortex and hippocampus in freely behaving adult male rats (v1.0)
description: Electrophysiological recordings using Neuropixels 2.0 multishank silicon probes were performed in the lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC), medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), and area CA1 of the hippocampus in freely behaving adult male rats. Of the nine total rats, three were implanted only in LEC, two were implanted in LEC and MEC, one was implanted in LEC and CA1, and three were implanted in all three brain areas. Rats performed a variety of behaviors with different degrees of event structure. These behaviors include sleep, open field foraging, lap running on a maze, and exploring novel objects in an open arena. The number of individual units recorded simultaneously was from a few hundred to over one thousand units per brain area. Data was obtained from each rat for approximately one week, after which the number of recorded units was too low for our purposes, particularly in LEC. Data include unit spike times, tracked position of the animal, and timestamps of scheduled events. These data could be reused for numerous purposes beyond the scope of the associated article, such as analysis of the coordination between brain areas during behavior.

name: Mapping of potentiated synapses in mouse hippocampus and organotypic hippocampal slices using SynActive constructs (v1)
description:
Synaptic engrams are defined as the neural population sustaining a given memory and they can be considered the cellular basis of learning processes characterized by newly formed spines. Nowadays there are no tools able to detect engrams at synaptic level.
We created a pair of Adeno Associate Viruses (AAV)-carried constructs to tag and visualize potentiated dendritic spines, in a spatially localized and activity-dependent manner. In a set of in vivo experiments, the pair was stereotaxically injected into the mouse hippocampus. Injected mice were exposed to contextual fear conditioning to trigger synaptic plasticity and potentiation. Confocal imaging of fixed brain sections allowed quantification of the distribution of potentiated spines along the dendritic tree of hippocampal pyramidal neurons. These data can be reused to implement computational models to infer synaptic plasticity rules leading to the formation of synaptic memory engrams.
Second, we infected organotypic hippocampal slices with the AAV pair and then stimulated with chemical long-term potentiation. Confocal imaging of fixed organotypic slices reveals a strong SynActive signal (potentiated synapses), partially merged with the not-potentiated spines only in infected-stimulated organotypic slices compared to their controls (not infected cultures or infected-not stimulated, thus showing the specificity of the SynActive signal in potentiated synapses.
Broadly, confocal imaging of fixed organotypic hippocampal slices allowed quantification of the distribution of potentiated spines along the dendritic tree of hippocampal pyramidal neurons. These data can be reused to implement computational models to infer synaptic plasticity rules leading to the formation of synaptic memory engrams.

name: Microscopic images showing the fibro- and cytoarchitecture demarcating the border between the dentate gyrus and CA3 in domestic pig (Sus scrofa domesticus) (v2)
description: This dataset from domestic pig (Sus scrofa domesticus) consists of a selection of bright-field microscopic images of thionin- and Timm-thionin-stained horizontal brain sections and Golgi-stained sections cut perpendicular to the long axis of the isolated hippocampus together elucidating part of the fibro- and cytoarchitecture of the hippocampal formation. The thionin-staining shows blue cell somata while the Timm-staining in addition exhibits the darkly stained zinc-containing axonal terminals that occur scattered throughout the entire length of both the main mossy fibres and their collaterals. Golgi-impregnated sections, that were cut transverse to the long axis of the isolated hippocampus, feature the morphology of randomly stained cell bodies and dendrites, as well as unmyelinated axons, including mossy fibres and their collaterals. This combination of staining methods provides cyto- and fibroarchitectonic features suitable for exploring the microscopic architecture and localizing the border between the dentate gyrus and cornu Ammonis 3 in pig.

name: Subcortical modulation of hippocampal activity, multichannel recordings in head-restrained, behaving mice (v1)
description:
Cortical circuits display different functional states under the influence of subcortical modulatory input. In our study we aimed to uncover fundamental aspects of this subcortical modulation by focusing on the effect of the median raphe (MR) nucleus on the hippocampal network. High channel count electrophysiological recordings were executed from dorsal hippocampus, along with the measurement of neuronal activity in the median raphe, in head-restrained, awake mice. The different cell types of the MR (vGAT, vGlut2, vGlut3) were optogenetically identified and multimodal sensory stimuli were applied to the mouse while monitoring both subcortical activity in the MR and activity in the dorsal CA1 region.

These data allow us to characterize the properties of hippocampal neurons in the intact animal and how these properties are changed by subcortical inputs thus providing important constraints for network models of the hippocampus.

name: Left-right-alternating theta sweeps in the entorhinal-hippocampal spatial map (v1)
description:
This dataset contains electrophysiological population recordings from 19 freely behaving rats implanted with high-site-count Neuropixels probes in the medial entorhinal cortex (n=10), the hippocampus (n=2), or both regions (n=7). Numbers of simultaneously recorded units ranges from 235-1,522. The recordings were obtained while the rats engaged in different navigational tasks (foraging in an open field; running in a wagon-wheel-shaped maze, an m-shaped maze, or a linear track), and during natural sleep in a rest chamber. The animals’ head positions and orientations were tracked with OptiTrack motion-capture system.

The raw neural activity was spike-sorted using Kilosort 2.5. The present data files include the spike-sorted activity (spike times) of all cells that were used in the accompanying paper. Grid cells were clustered into ‘modules’ according to their spatial firing patterns.

The data may be used to examine activity of spatial-coding neural populations (or single cells) during navigation and sleep.

name: Optimized SynActive tools to study structure and function of potentiated synapses (v2)
description:
Synaptic engrams can be defined as the synapse population of neurons supporting a specific memory and are believed to represent the cellular basis of learning processes characterized by newly formed or potentiated spines. We developed a new platform (SA =SynActive toolbox) in which a prototypical pair of SA constructs was employed to tag and visualize translation-dependent potentiated dendritic spines, in a spatially localized and activity-dependent manner ([Gobbo et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-017-01699-7), [Gobbo et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnmol.2020.572312)).

We created a series of new Adeno Associated Viruses (AAV)-derived constructs: 1) SA-eGRASP; 2) PHP.eB-SA; 3) AAV9-SA. Such vectors represent a fundamental advancement as compared with the original SA constructs both in terms of spatial resolution and in view of in vitro and in vivo use for specific CNS targeting.

The new pair was stereotaxically injected into the hippocampus. Injected mice were exposed to contextual fear conditioning to trigger synaptic plasticity and translation-dependent long-term potentiation (LTP) of synapses. We also infected organotypic hippocampal slices with the appropriate AAV pair, before stimulating with chemical or electrical LTP. 

A specific SA signal (identifying translation-dependent potentiated synapses) was revealed following confocal imaging of hippocampus from perfused mice and fixed organotypic slices. Potentiated spines along the dendritic tree of hippocampal pyramidal neurons were quantified and their distribution was investigated. All these new datasets can be exploited for computational models of synaptic memory engrams.

Group A: Dataset from the SA-eGRASP experiments include 3 images from 1 slice from 3 separate mice that underwent the association phase of the contextual fear conditioning while injected with doxycycline, 1 image from 1 slice of 1 mouse that was injected with doxycycline but remained in their homecage, and 1 image from 1 slice from 1 mouse that underwent the association phase of the contextual fear conditioning protocol but was not injected with doxycycline.

Version 2: An additional image from a mouse showing synaptic potentiation during the re-exposure phase of the contextual fear conditioning paradigm, i.e. re-exposure to the context the day following the association phase, with doxycycline injections shifted. 

Group B: Data from PhP.eB SA-venus experiments include 3 images from 3 different mice that underwent the association phase of the contextual fear conditioning paradigm, injected with doxycycline and with immunofluorescence done against Venus. Of these, the first mouse was injected with concentrations: Filler 1:120 (1.14x108vg) & SA-venus 1:16 (8.75x107vg), the second mouse injected with concentrations: filler 1:120 (1.14x108vg) & SA-venus 1:8 (1.75x108vg), the third mouse injected with concentration: filler 1:20 (6.82x108vg) & SA-Venus 1:8 (1.75x108vg (1:8). 1 image comes from a mouse that was injected with concentrations: filler 1:120 (1.14x108vg) & SA-venus 1:8 (1.75x108vg), but did not receive any doxycycline and remained in its homecage. name: Hippocampal subfields revealed through unfolding and unsupervised clustering of laminar and morphological features in 3D BigBrain (v1)
description:
The internal structure of the human hippocampus is challenging to map using histology or neuroimaging due to its complex archicortical folding. Here, we aimed to overcome this challenge using a unique combination of three methods. First, we leveraged a histological dataset with unprecedented 3D coverage, BigBrain. Second, we imposed a computational unfolding framework that respects the topological continuity of hippocampal subfields, which are traditionally defined by laminar composition. Third, we adapted neocortical parcellation techniques to map the hippocampus with respect to not only laminar but also morphological features. Unsupervised clustering of these features revealed subdivisions that closely resemble gold standard manual subfield segmentations. Critically, we also show that morphological features alone are sufficient to derive most hippocampal subfield boundaries. Moreover, some features showed differences within subfields along the hippocampal longitudinal axis. Our findings highlight new characteristics of internal hippocampal structure, and offer new avenues for its characterization with in-vivo neuroimaging [DeKraker et al. 2020]. **For methodological details, see**: DeKraker, J., Lau, J. name: 3D reconstructions of human hippocampal pyramidal cells and spiny striatum cells (v1)
description: Pyramidal neurons are the most common cell type and are considered the main output neuron in most mammalian forebrain structures. In terms of function, differences in the structure of the dendrites of these neurons appear to be crucial in determining how neurons integrate information. To further shed light on the structure of the human pyramidal neurons, in the present project we investigated the geometry of pyramidal cells in different regions of the human hippocampal formation (CA1 field distal, CA2 field, CA3 field, and subiculum) and spiny cells of the striatum.  Over 100 intracellularly injected cells were 3D-reconstructed cells from 3D confocal stack of images, using Neurolucida software. Quantitative information about several relevant features of neurons, such as the extension and branching patterns of their dendritic trees and local axonal arbors were analyzed. 3D reconstructions of human cells, and the corresponding morphological features extracted, will be useful for modeling and integration of anatomical data with functional studies in different brain regions such as the hippocampus and striatum.
new_in_this_version: This dataset contains 102 3D reconstructions of the human CA1 distal field (n=20), CA2 field (n=15), CA3 field (n=25), and subiculum (n=25) cells from the hippocampal formation; and striatal projection neurons(n=15) from the putamen.

name: Electrophysiological recordings of hippocampal CA1 units in rats during open field foraging (v1.0)
description: This dataset contains electrophysiological recordings of more than a thousand single units from the hippocampal subfield Cornu Ammonis 1 of 5 male Long Evans rats, obtained while the animals foraged for chocolate cereal crumbs in a 150x150 cm (squared) open field arena. The units were recorded during a total of 114 sessions—all of which lasted for at least twenty minutes or longer. The data was collected to investigate the possible occurrence of egocentric tuning in hippocampal neurons in rats. Well-trained rats were chronically implanted with drives that guided tetrode electrodes into the target brain region and local field potentials were recorded using either a AxonaLtd daqUSB or Neuralynx system; in both cases with an overhead camera tracking two LEDs on the head stage of the animal to register the 2D position of the animal. The data may be used to investigate the spatial properties of CA1 cells in the non-changing standard “open field session”.
new_in_this_version: This dataset contains recordings of approximately 1000 single units recorded from the hippocampal CA1 field in 5 male Long Evans rats. The data were collected during 114 open field sessions in a 150x150 cm arena—familiar to the animals—while the animals foraged for chocolate treats. This is the first version of this dataset.

name: Mechanistic analysis of ERP in rodents (v1)
description:
The aim of this task is to gain a better understanding on the nature of the evoked related potentials (ERPs) induced by a current stimulation of the secondary motor cortex (M2), which has been adopted for generating the cortical perturbation in task PCI-like measure in rodents.

Since a current stimulation is not physiological, it can be difficult to predict the exact brain response. We, therefore, stimulated M2 of head-restrained awake rats with current pulses of different intensities, in order to approximate a stimulus-response function. We repeated these measures during general anaesthesia to verify if differences in the ERPs could be trivially explained by reduced brain excitability induced by the anaesthetic compound. We then explored the extension of the brain areas that are recruited in the response by simultaneously recording from several cortical regions and from the hippocampus, by mean of chronically implanted stainless-steel and tungsten electrodes respectively.

name: Characterization of human hippocampal neurons and interneurons using single-cell RNA-seq (V1)
description: The goal was to define the cellular heterogeneity in the human dentate gyrus (DG) and delineate this from the cellular architecture in the Cornu Ammonis (CA) region. Therefore, after isolation of NeunN-expressing nuclei from fresh-frozen hippocampal tissues (DG and CA), nuclei were used to generate single-cell transcriptomes using a commercial microwell-based assay. After library preparation and sequencing, the generated data were further processed and aligned against the reference genome. Gene expression matrixes are provided which can be further analyzed and overlaid with synaptic maps and organization, microanatomical and physiological data, and integrated for the generation of a human brain atlas.

name: NLG3KO mice exhibit deficits in social behavior (v1)
description:
Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) comprise a heterogeneous group of neuro-developmental abnormalities with a strong genetic component, characterized by deficits in verbal and non-verbal communication, impaired social interactions, and stereotyped behaviors. In a small percentage of cases, ASDs are associated with alterations of genes involved in synaptic function. Among  these, relatively frequent are mutations/deletions of genes encoding for neuroligins (NLGs). NLGs are postsynaptic adhesion molecules that,  interacting with their presynaptic partners neurexins, ensure the cross talk between pre- and postsynaptic specializations and synaptic stabilization, a condition needed for maintaining a proper excitatory/inhibitory balance within local neuronal circuits.
We have focused on mice lacking NLG3 (NLG3 knock-out mice), animal models of a non-syndromic form of autism, which exhibit deficits in social behavior reminiscent of those found in ASDs.
Data obtained in our experiments can be used by researchers to understand social deficits induced by lack of Neuroligin 3 protein.

name: Excitability of mouse hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons during sustained (500 ms) strong depolarization (v1)
description:
In this work, we highlight an electrophysiological feature often observed in recordings from mouse CA1 pyramidal cells that has so far been ignored by experimentalists and modelers. It consists of a large and dynamic increase in the depolarization baseline (i.e., the minimum value of the membrane potential between successive action potentials during a sustained depolarizing input) in response to strong somatic current injections. Such an increased sustained depolarization can directly affect neurotransmitter release properties and, more generally, the efficacy of synaptic transmission. However, it cannot be explained by any currently available conductance-based computational model.

Here, we provide the original data describing and modeling the depolarization baseline (DBL) phenomenon and descriptions of the methods used, as reported in the related publication (Bianchi et al., 2022). This dataset entails the experiments generated in laboratory 2.

name: X-ray virtual histology for the investigation of temporal lobe epilepsy in a mouse model (v1)
description: This study evaluates virtual histology with synchrotron radiation-based X-ray microtomography to track the histopathological progression of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (mTLE) in a mouse model. The kainate (KA) model of mTLE is used, where stereotactic KA injection into the hippocampus induces a pathological phenotype resembling that in humans. Label-free X-ray virtual histology with 1.6 μm-wide voxels was used to image paraffin-embedded brain hemispheres from mice sacrificed 1, 7, 14, and 21 days after KA injection. The onset of hippocampal sclerosis, namely granule cell dispersion and pyramidal neuron loss, could be identified with virtual histology. The volumetric virtual histology data were benchmarked against corresponding sections in conventional histology. Finally, automatic segmentation of the molecular, granular, and polymorph layers of the dentate gyrus with a deep convolutional neural network enabled three-dimensional quantification of electron density and morphology changes during epileptogenesis.

description: Modern modelling and simulation approaches have been exploited to pinpoint and design more potent and specific ligands and allosteric modulators which can be used not only for research, but also for diagnostic and even therapeutic purposes. name: Hippocampal place cell recordings in a Four-Room navigation task (v1)
description: Hippocampal place cells show location-specific firing and are thought to be an essential component of the brain’s “cognitive map”, supporting flexible memorization of places and possibly of their connectivity. So far, only a few studies investigated whether these cells encode the connectivity between places, either by adding a barrier or removing a wall. We aimed to go one step further and investigated whether place cells can encode pure connectivity, i.e. changes in the “closed” or “open” aspect of an otherwise identical door. We performed extracellular tetrode recordings from the dorsal CA1 hippocampus of 5 male Lister-Hooded rats while they were foraging and navigating in a 4-compartment environment. Pushable doors were used by the rats to transition between compartments. At first, all 4 doors were pushable. In a test condition, either one of the doors was closed, or all of the doors were closed one-way. This data could be analysed further to investigate basic place cell firing properties as well as possible neural correlates of navigation in such an environment.

name: Stimulation of the ventral tegmental area in macaques drives category-selective learning in the absence of attention (v1)
description: Perception improves by repeated practice with visual stimuli, a phenomenon known as visual perceptual learning (VPL). The interplay of attentional and  neuromodulatory reward signals is hypothesized to cause these behavioral and associated neuronal changes, although VPL can occur without attention (i.e. task-irrelevant VPL). In addition, task-relevant VPL can be category-selective for simple attended oriented stimuli. Yet, it is unclear whether category-selective task-irrelevant VPL occurs, nor which brain centers mediate underlying form of adult cortical plasticity. Here, we show that pairing sublaminal complex visual stimuli (faces and bodies) with electrical microstimulation of the ventral tegmental area (VTA-EM) causes category-selective task-irrelevant VPL. These perceptual improvements are accompanied by fMRI signal changes in early and late visual and frontal areas, as well as the cerebellum, hippocampus, claustrum and putamen. In conclusion, Pavlovian pairing of unattended complex stimuli with VTA-EM causes category-selective learning accompanied by changes of cortical and subcortical neural representations in macaques.

name: Human ultra-high resolution functional imaging data (7 Tesla) on multi-element event memories (general raw data) (v1)
description:
Ultra-high resolution 7Tesla functional MRI data (0.8 mm isotropic) was acquired in 30 young, healthy adults. During data acquisition, participants performed the encoding and retrieval phase of a memory task. Participants learned events, consisting of a popular person, an object (or animal) and a location in a pairwise associative manner. At retrieval, in a 4-alternative forced choice recognition task, one event element served as a cue while a belonging target element was presented among familiar lures of the same element type (e.g. location). Each event was cued from all directions. A closed loop structure (AB-BC-BA) versus an open loop structure (AB-BC-CD) was employed by half of the events, respectively, at encoding.
Functional data captured a slice, oriented along the longitudinal axis of the hippocampus and covered the medial temporal lobe, superior occipital cortices and parietal regions. Structural T2-weighted (slice) and T1-weighted data (whole-brain) was acquired. Data can be reused to answer questions about the functional involvement of medial temporal lobe subregions, structure-behavior relationships, questions about memory formation and retrieval.

name: Human functional imaging data (7 Tesla) on learning audiovisual scene-object associations (v1)
description:
MRI data at 7Tesla was acquired in 24 healthy adults. During functional data acquisition, participants learned and retrieved scene-object associations of which either element was an auditory or a visual stimulus. Initially, single elements are presented as unimodal stimuli. Thereafter, audiovisual scene-object associations are learned. In a subsequent recall, cued by one element, the paired element had to be vividly imagined. After MRI data acquisition, all audiovisual scene-object associations were tested based on the auditory cue and the visual cue, respectively, in a behavioral 4-alternative-forced-choice recognition task and a questionnaire. 
Functional data captured a slab (resolution: 1mm isotropic), which was oriented along the longitudinal axis of the hippocampus and covering the temporal lobe, auditory cortex, superior occipital cortices and parietal regions. Structural T2-weighted (slab, resolution: 0.4x0.4x1mm) and T1-weighted data (whole-brain, resolution: 0.8mm isotropic) was acquired. Data can be reused to answer questions about the functional involvement of medial temporal lobe subregions, their neocortical interactions, structure-behavior relationships, and questions about multisensory integration and memory formation.

name: Longitudinal imaging and LFP data from visPOR across learning, with offline manipulation of neural activity in parvalbumin expressing neurons (v1)
description: This dataset contains behavioural and imaging data from two-photon Ca2+ imaging and LFP neurophysiological recordings related to mechanisms of learning and memory consolidation. Neural activity of 13 adult PV-Cre male mice was recorded across training for 10 sessions (days) from naive to expert performance. Each session consisted of baseline, training and post-training rest recordings. In addition, 8 mice were only used for behaviour. Two groups of mice were used, expressing either DIO-hM4Di-mCherry or inert Flex-mRuby3 bilaterally in visPOR by local virus injections. Each session consisted of 6 single runs. The mice were injected with 5 mg/kg Clozapine-N-Oxide (CNO) between the end of run 3 and the beginning of run 9. In between these runs the animals could consume a high-calorie milkshake ad-libitum for 30 minutes. In mice used in imaging and LFP, CNO injections were done in the odd sessions for each mouse. On even days, saline was injected. In mice only used for behaviour the odd/even CNO injections were randomized between individuals. LFP was only recorded in runs 9 and 10. Data of all 6 daily runs are included in this dataset, including the behavior recordings from imaging mice. These recordings can be used to further analyse the contribution of parvalbumin-expressing interneurons in learning and during spontaneous cortical activity before and after training.

name: Electrophysiological characterization of sharp-wave ripple oscillations and associated cellular activities in hippocampal slices from Scn1a+/- mice (v1)
description: The data was obtained from hippocampal area CA1 in acute hippocampal slices from transgenic _Scn1a<sup>+/-</sup>_ mice and wild type littermates. The dataset consists of field potential recordings, simultaneous field and somatic whole cell patch clamp recordings from either fast-spiking parvalbumin-expressing cells or from pyramidal cells, only somatic recordings, and axonal whole cell patch clamp recordings. Data was collected for two age groups, juvenile mice (age range postnatal days 19-23) before the critical period of high mortality of the _Scn1a<sup>+/-</sup>_ genotype, and young adult mice (age range postnatal days 28-37) surviving past the critical period. Accordingly, the data is organised into four different groups throughout the dataset. Field potential recordings were used to quantify sharp wave ripple oscillation activity and to relate ripple oscillations to synaptic and action potential activity recorded from individual cells in the temporal domain. Somatic recordings were used to quantify the amplitude of synaptic currents and to study action potential timing and waveform. Axon recordings were used to quantify action potential waveforms only. The data can be reused to analyse the interplay between field and (sub-)cellular activity of different cell types in the hippocampus.

name: Adaptive modulation of theta sweeps in the brain’s spatial navigation circuit (v1)
description:
This dataset contains electrophysiological population recordings from 10 freely behaving rats implanted with high-site-count Neuropixels probes. All animals were implanted in the medial entorhinal cortex and parasubiculum (MEC-parasubiculum); subsets were additionally implanted in hippocampus, presubiculum, anterodorsal thalamus and/or postrhinal cortex, with up to four probes per animal. The recordings were obtained while the rats engaged in different navigational tasks (free foraging in an open-field arena; pursuit of a rapidly moving bait in the same arena; running on a linear track; backing out of narrow corridors or across the open field) and during natural sleep in a rest chamber, including periods of REM sleep. The animals’ head position and direction were tracked with an OptiTrack motion-capture system, and bait position was tracked using OptiTrack or DeepLabCut.

The raw neural activity was spike-sorted using Kilosort 2.5. The present data files include the spike-sorted activity (spike times) of all cells used in the accompanying paper, and grid cells in MEC-parasubiculum are clustered into modules according to their spatial firing patterns.

The data may be used to examine activity of spatially modulated and direction-tuned neural populations during free exploration, goal-directed pursuit, backward locomotion and sleep.

name: Electrophysiological properties and spontaneous synaptic activity in developing mouse CA1 neurons (v1)
description: This dataset was created to characterize the postnatal development of electrophysiological properties and spontaneous excitatory synaptic activity in C57BL/6J mouse hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons. Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were obtained from acute hippocampal slices prepared from 52 animals of both sexes across four postnatal age groups: P4-P6 (P5), P8-P9 (P8), P13-P16 (P15), and P19-P23 (P21). In total, the dataset contains recordings from 256 neurons, with 1-15 neurons recorded per animal. Two main types of electrophysiological recordings are included. Under current-clamp conditions, neuronal voltage responses to subthreshold and suprathreshold current steps ranging from -60 to 390 pA were recorded to capture membrane responses, individual action potentials, and repetitive firing. Under voltage-clamp conditions, spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents were recorded for ~6-10 min while neurons were held at -70 mV. The dataset contains raw electrophysiological recordings in Axon Binary File (.abf) format. These data can be reused to investigate passive membrane properties, action potential characteristics, neuronal excitability and firing patterns, spontaneous excitatory synaptic activity, and age- or sex-related variation during early postnatal hippocampal development.
new_in_this_version: This is the first version of the dataset, prepared following an initial review and quality assessment of the recordings. It contains whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from 256 hippocampal CA1 neurons obtained from 52 mice of both sexes across four postnatal age groups (P5, P8, P15, P21). The dataset includes raw current-clamp recordings of membrane responses and evoked action potential firing, as well as voltage-clamp recordings of spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents. Prior to release, the recordings underwent quality control, and recordings that were incomplete, affected by excessive noise that could not be corrected, or otherwise unsuitable for reliable downstream analysis were excluded. This version therefore contains the curated set of electrophysiological recordings selected for quantitative analysis.

name: Patch-clamp electrophysiological characterization of neurons in human dentate gyrus (V1)
description: The dentate gyrus (DG) is a substructure within the hippocampal formation that is crucial to memory processing through its cell types and projections. However, much less is known about the correlation between these characteristics and genetic expression. Together with our partners, we aimed at characterizing genetic expression in human and murine DG. For the first phase of this project, we performed experiments in a total of 9 brain samples, deriving 40 usable cells that were recorded using patch-clamp (whole-cell, current-clamp), 26 of which had their cytoplasm collected for further analysis. This preliminary study showed that we have the technical ability to perform patch-seq at a possible rate of success of around 80%, since 21/26 cells that had their cytoplasm collected contained enough detectable RNA content to suggest further sequencing was possible. The data we are sharing represents the patch-clamp experiments performed during this first stage of the project. It includes the recordings of 40 cells from human brain tissue which underwent our full characterization protocol.

name: Microscopic images showing the fibro- and cytoarchitecture demarcating the border between the dentate gyrus and CA3 in sheep (Ovis aries) (v2)
description: This dataset from sheep (Ovis aries) consists of a selection of bright-field microscopic images of Timm-thionin- and Golgi-stained histological sections from alternating blocks cut transverse to the long axis of the isolated hippocampi. Timm-thionin-stained sections show blue cell somata and black zinc-containing axonal terminals that occur scattered along the entire length of both main mossy fibres and their collaterals thus making them traceable, although the fibres themselves remain largely unstained. Golgi-impregnated sections show the morphology of randomly stained cell bodies and dendrites with postsynaptic excrescences, as well as unmyelinated axons, including mossy fibres and their collaterals with presynaptic boutons and varicosities. This combination of staining methods provides cyto- and fibroarchitectonic features suitable for exploring the microscopic architecture and localizing the border between the dentate gyrus and cornu Ammonis 3.

name: Activity-dependent changes of spine proteomes (v1)
description:
It is well established that synapses undergo activity-dependent changes in their synaptic strength. The weakening or strengthening of synapses is driven by translational and/or post-translational changes in their proteins composition, the so-called “synaptic proteome”.  Its composition is highly dynamic both in basal condition and as a result of synaptic activity. Therefore, acquisition of data on the proteomic changes underlying synaptic plasticity is crucial to properly understand the molecular mechanisms by which these organelles modify their weight according to activity. Although it is possible to obtain the proteomic profile of synaptic proteins from a bunch of different preparations (Sharma et al., 2015; Biesmann et al., 2013; Distler et al., 2014; Loh 2016) these methods do not allow to specifically detecting proteomic changes in activated synapses. Hence, with this study we aim at providing a pilot proteome dataset from hippocampal activated synapses by taking advantages of a recently developed activity-dependent synaptic expression vector . The method is based on the new expression vector pSYNACTIVE (Gobbo et al., 2017) that allows to achieve the activity dependent translation of reporter proteins at activated dendritic spines. This is possible as the pSYNACTIVE vector exploits the 5’UTR and 3’UTR RNA sequences of Arc/Arg3.1 mRNA and a PSD-targeting protein sequence fused to the report (Gobbo et al., 2017).
The experimental approach we propose has several advantages over the existing methods as it allows to: i) correlating protein abundance in activated synapses with the strengthening of excitatory synapses; ii) obtaining the functional mapping of activated synapses. By doing so it is possible to establish how different pattern of activity may activate different subset of excitatory synapses.

name: Functional imaging data (3 Tesla) on Object-In-Room Recall in healthy, younger adults (v1)
description: Episodic memories comprise information from various domains (e.g. objects and scenes). Upon retrieval, a unimodal cue can be sufficient to reinstate the multimodal representation of the episode. Here, functional neuroimaging data at 3Tesla was acquired in 25 healthy adults. Participants learned object-in-room associations. Each artificially created room contained two objects at random locations. During functional data acquisition, participants were cued with empty rooms and a specific object location, upon which they were required to recall and imagine the respective object and indicate whether the room was old or new. A subsequent 3 alternative forced choice recognition task assessed whether the object they remembered in that location was the correct object, the other object within that room or a third, familiar object that has not been paired with that room. A control condition contained empty rooms only. Here, participants perceptually matched room-cut-outs to a specific location within a novel empty room. Functional data captured a slab (resolution: 1.8x1.8x1.8 mm), oriented along the longitudinal axis of the hippocampus and covered the temporal lobe, parietal and visual cortex and inferior frontal regions. Structural T2-weighted (slab, resolution: 0.4x0.4x1mm) and T1-weighted data (whole-brain, resolution: 0.6mm3) was acquired. Data can be used to answer questions about the functional involvement of medial temporal lobe subregions, their neocortical interactions, structure-behavior relationships, and questions about context-object retrieval and memory recollection.

name: Optimization of single neuron models for CA1 hippocampal neurons in rat (v4.0.5)
description:
We developed a library of single neuron models for rat CA1 hippocampal neurons. The model morphologies were based on three-dimensional morphological reconstructions obtained in a previous study. Electrophysiological features of interest were extracted from experimental traces using custom code exploiting the open source Electrophysiological Feature Extraction Library (eFEL). Extracted features were then used for multi-objective model parameter optimizations performed using the open source Blue Brain Python Optimization Library (BluePyOpt).

Entries for the individual models are available in the EBRAINS repository. This dataset groups the code for all models, together with all outputs from the optimization process.

name: Dendritic morphologies of four groups of mouse hippocampal interneurons (v1)
description: Computational modelling of hippocampal network mechanisms requires real-life morphological features of the dendritic arbors of interneurons (INs) in the CA1 area. There are several different groups of hippocampal interneurons. We investigated four groups. Hippocampo-septal (HS) INs project both locally and to the medial septum. Oriens-lacunosum-moleculare (OLM) INs are typical local feedback inhibitory neurons. Parvalbumin (PV)- and calretinin (CR)-containing INs represent two different groups of local INs. Here, using viral tracing and immunohistochemistry, we labeled these classes of INs and using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), we measured their dendritic cross-sectional areas and perimeters along the dendritic segments of these neurons. We estimated their volumes with and without mitochondria and estimated their dendritic surface areas as well. We measured and corrected all changes during tissue processing, therefore, all physical parameters represent the real life parameters of these dendrites.

name: Modulation of hippocampal GABAergic currents by anti-gephyrin intrabodies (delta2-188) (v1)
description:
The efficiency of synaptic transmission relies on the temporally and spatially regulated expression of postsynaptic receptors localized in precise apposition to presynaptic release sites. At synapses, receptors are organized in clusters which are formed by highly regulated events, dynamically controlled by a number of proteins including scaffolds, adhesion molecules and active transport processes along the cytoskeleton (Kneussel and Loebrich, 2007).

At inhibitory synapses, GABAergic signaling controls dendritic integration, neural excitability, circuit reorganization and fine tuning of network activity. Among different players, the tubulin-binding protein gephyrin, plays a key role in anchoring GABAA receptors to synaptic membranes, (Tyagarajan and Fritschy, 2014). Moreover, gephyrin is instrumental in establishing and maintaining a proper excitatory (E)/inhibitory (I) balance necessary for the correct functioning of neuronal networks (Pizzarelli and Cherubini, 2011). A disruption of the E/I balance is thought to be at the origin of several neuropsychiatric disorders including epilepsy, schizophrenia and autism (Penzes et al. 2013; Cellot and Cherubini, 2014; Nelson and Valakh, 2015).

We tested the effects of truncated form of gephyrin (delta 2-188), acting as a dominant negative protein, on spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents, sIPSCs, from hippocampal neurons in culture.  In cells transfected with delta 2-188 fused to EGFP or with EGFP alone, the mean sIPSCs frequency was 0.91 ± 0.18 Hz in control (n=10) and 0.42 ± 0.09 Hz in the presence of delta 2-188 (n=9). The mean sIPSCs amplitude was 129.4 ± 18.8 pA in controls and 81.9 ±m13.2 pA in the presence of delta 2-188. Significant differences were found between controls and delta 2-188 regarding the frequency and amplitude of sIPSCs (p=0.03 and p=0.05, respectively). These data further support the hypothesis that gephyrin regulates the postsynaptic organization of synaptic GABAA receptors.

name: sIPSCs from juvenile (P21-30) C57B16/J male mice from hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons receiving input from PV+ and CCK+ interneurons (v1)
description:
A general procedure to fit individual synaptic events recorded from voltage clamp experiments was tested with various sets of experimental data on GABAergic synapses; gephyrin and gephyrin-dependent pathways were chosen as a suitable example of a kinetic model of synaptic transmission. The data used here are obtained from coronal hippocampal slices (300 μm thick) from juvenile (P21-30) C57B16/J male mice and recorded from hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons receiving input from parvalbumin positive (PV+) and cholecystokinin positive (CCK+) interneurons. The dataset contains 2130 individual events recorded from 3 different neurons (expD1-D3). The first column of each txt file contains the time in ms and the other columns contain spontaneous inhibitory synaptic currents (sIPSCs) in pA.
Computational modeling of brain circuits requires the definition of many parameters that are difficult to determine from experimental findings. One way to help interpret these data is to fit them using a particular kinetic model. In [1] we proposed a general procedure to fit individual synaptic events recorded from voltage clamp experiments. Starting from any given model description (mod file) in the NEURON simulation environment, the procedure exploits user-defined constraints, dependencies, and rules for the parameters of the model to fit the time course of individual spontaneous synaptic events that are recorded experimentally. A Python version is available for public use, as a Jupyter Notebook in the Collaboratory Portal of the Human Brain Project. To illustrate the potential application of the procedure, we tested its use with various sets of experimental data on GABAergic synapses; gephyrin and gephyrin-dependent pathways were chosen as a suitable example of a kinetic model of synaptic transmission. For individual spontaneous inhibitory events in hippocampal pyramidal CA1 neurons, we found that gephyrin-dependent subcellular pathways may shape synaptic events at different levels, and can be correlated with cell- or event-specific activity history and/or pathological conditions.
Fitting experimental data against a number of different models is a common way to do this (reviewed in [2]), and can help in the subsequent interpretation of the data. In general, experimental traces are fitted using specific approaches for specific purposes (e.g., [3], [4]). However, to the best of our knowledge, there is no easy, user-friendly, general procedure available for this purpose, especially in computational neuroscience. Our aim was thus to identify the appropriate conceptual structure of a procedure to obtain good, reliable fits of raw experimental traces of spontaneous synaptic events. This is an important step because spontaneous synaptic events have been so far exclusively analyzed using traces obtained by averaging many events. However, as can be easily imagined, each synapse in any given neuron has its own, independent, history of activation. The most likely physiological consequence is that the variables relative to the subcellular processes underlying synaptic transmission are different for each synapse. If a researcher is interested in testing a specific kinetic scheme implemented for specific biochemical pathways, the use of individual events is the most appropriate choice, since this approach would give information on the different combinations of model parameters that are consistent with the observed events. Averaging traces will lose a lot of relevant information.
We therefore present here the implementation of a procedure leading to the development of a unifying optimization method for individual synaptic events. Experimental data, kinetic models of synaptic transmission, and fitting parameters and their dependencies can be user defined/provided or gathered from databases. They can be used to generate optimized groups of parameters able to represent a population of synapses, either for simulation purposes or to study the functional consequences of a particular protein or subcellular synaptic transmission pathway.

[2] Van Geit W., De Schutter E., Achard P. (2008). Automated neuron model optimization techniques: a review. Biol. Cybern. 99, 241–251. 10.1007/s00422-008-0257-6  
[3] Bekkers J. M. (2003). Convolution of mini distributions for fitting evoked synaptic amplitude histograms. J. Neurosci. Methods. 130, 105–114. 10.1016/j.jneumeth.2003.09.018

name: Spike time dependent plasticity (STDP) data from neonate C57BL/6 (wild-type) mice, positive pairing (v1)
description:
Spike-time dependent plasticity (STDP is a particular form of Hebbian type of learning which consists in bidirectional modifications of synaptic strength according to the temporal order of pre- and postsynaptic spiking (*Dan Y1, Poo MM (2006) Spike timing-dependent plasticity: from synapse to perception. Physiol Rev 86:1033-1048*). Thus, positively correlated pre- and postsynaptic spiking (pre before post) within a critical window leads to long term potentiation (LTP), whereas a negative correlation (post before pre) leads to long term depression (LTD).  
At the neonatal stage, the hippocampal mossy fiber (MF)-CA3 is GABAergic and exhibits STDP. Our data demonstrate that, at the same age, positive pairing fails to induce STD-LTP at MF-CA3 synapses in hippocampal slices obtained from neuroligin-3 (NL3) knock-in (NL3<sup>R451C</sup>KI) and NL3 knock-out (KO) mice. Similarly, in NLR<sup>R451C</sup> KI mice, negative pairing failed to cause STD-LTD. In contrast, STD-LTP and STD-LTD can be readily produced in control age-matched WT littermates. In NLR<sup>R451C</sup> KI  mice, the impairment in STD-LTP is maintained in adulthood when MF are glutamatergic. This set of data refers to the neonate, C57BL/6 (wild-type), positive pairing condition.

name: Regional and laminar distribution of receptors for glutamate in the rat brain (v2)
description: The present dataset provides the quantitative regional and laminar distribution of key molecules of excitatory neurotransmission, namely the ionotropic glutamate receptors AMPA, kainate and NMDA, in five selected rostrocaudal levels of the rat brain. The receptors were visualized by means of quantitative *in vitro* receptor autoradiography and the selective tritiated ligands AMPA, kainate and MK-801. The high spatial resolution of this method enables quantification of receptor densities in anatomically identifiable cortical structures as detailed as the hippocampal regions and layers, or subcortical structures such as amygdalar nuclei. We also provide information about image data registration to the Waxholm Sprague Dawley rat brain atlas.
new_in_this_version: This is the second version of the dataset containing in addition to the original files, the color-coded images of the linearized images provided in Version 1. It also contains the image registration files.

name: Multiplane microscopic atlas of rat brain zincergic terminal fields and metal-containing glia stained with Timm’s sulphide silver method (v1)
description: The dataset comprises high-resolution bright-field microscopy images of coronal, horizontal and sagittal serial rat brain sections in which zincergic terminal fields and metal-containing glia are visualised. The historical histological material was originally prepared to map the presence of zinc and heavy metals in the adult Wistar rat brain, and especially in the hippocampal formation. Alternating sections were stained with the Timm-Haug73 modification of the Timm’s sulphide silver method or Nissl staining for cytoarchitecture. The images are suitable as a microscopic reference resource for studies of terminal fields of zincergic fibre systems, and sulphide silver stained neuronal perikarya and glial cells, and as a general histological reference for researchers interested in normal rat brain architecture.

name: Synapse maps - FIBSEM (v1)
description: We have processed brain material from transgenic mice expressing the enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) coupled with the synaptic protein PSD95 (EGFP95) in order to accomplish the automated counting process using 3D connected components of fluorescent puncta in stacks of confocal microscope images for the CA1 region of the hippocampal formation. Adjacent brain sections have been processed with 3D electron microscopy using FIB/SEM in order to cross-validate and interpret confocal data with ultrastructural data on the number and size of PSD puncta in different brain regions. Furthermore, we have developed a PSDs volume segmentation and quantification algorithm designed to be executed in a supercomputer in order to obtain results in multiple brain regions in a short time.

name: Spatial navigation in virtual reality (v1)
description:
We present a mouse virtual reality (VR) system which restrains head-movements to horizontal rotations, potentially compatible with multi-photon imaging. This system allows expression of the spatial navigation and neuronal firing patterns characteristic of real open arenas.

This dataset contains electrophysiology recordings of hippocampal cells while animals were navigating in virtual environments. Each recording session consisted of one 40 min random-foraging trial in a virtual reality (VR) square environment and one 20 min trial in a real environment. 

Spike sorting was performed offline using an automated clustering algorithm (KlustaKwick) followed by a manual review and editing step using an interactive graphical tool (WAVEFORM by D. Manson, http://d1manson.github.io/waveform/). Spatial cells including place cells and grid cells have been identified in the dataset.

description:
This dataset contains quantitative data extracted from four sets of parvalbumin stained sections covering the whole brain of normal, adult Sprague-Dawley rats. Section images from the dataset “Distribution of parvalbumin-positive interneurons in the normal adult rat brain” [1] were analysed using the QUINT workflow. name: Synapse maps - confocal (v1)
description: We have processed brain material from transgenic mice expressing the enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) coupled with the synaptic protein PSD95 (EGFP95) in order to accomplish the automated counting process using 3D connected components of fluorescent puncta in stacks of confocal microscope images for the CA1 region of the hippocampal formation. Furthermore, we have developed a PSDs volume segmentation and quantification algorithm designed to be executed in a supercomputer in order to obtain results in multiple brain regions in a short time. We have currently uploaded 6 examples of the 3D automated counting process of the PSD95 protein using confocal microscopy, from the following CA1 regions: stratum oriens (SO), CA1 stratum radiatum (SR), CA1 stratum lacunosum moleculare (SLM). We have currently uploaded 1 example of the 3D counting process of PSD puncta using FIB/SEM from the CA1 SR region.

name: GPS-linked momentary assessment data with MRI, cognition, and mental health from young adults sharing residential environment (v1)
description: We present a cross-sectional dataset of 94 university students (mean=24.9 +/- 4 years, range 18–38 years, 42 women) who relocated from 43 different countries to a shared student housing facility in Berlin, Germany. Participants underwent structural and functional MRI scanning (T1-weighted MPRAGE, high-resolution PD-weighted hippocampal imaging, resting-state fMRI, and two task-based fMRI) and an extensive behavioural assessment. Psychological and environmental data were obtained through multiple questionnaires covering (1) early life and background, (2) lifestyle and daily activities, (3) psychological assessments, and (4) environmental assessments. In addition, participants completed a week-long geographical ecological momentary assessment (GEMA), during which they carried a mobile device that continuously tracked spatial location and delivered prompts at multiple time points per day for self-reports and cognitive tasks. This multimodal dataset integrates neuroimaging, self-report, cognitive, and real-world geospatial measures within a standardized residential environment. We provide detailed information on study design, data acquisition, and assessment protocols. The dataset offers a resource for investigating the dynamic interplay between environmental exposures, brain measures, and mental health, and supports research in the emerging field of Environmental Neuroscience.

name: High-resolution coronal sections of mouse brain with neuron segmentation and feature extraction (v1)
description:
This dataset comprises ten high-resolution images of coronal sections of a mouse brain located in antero-posterior hippocampal region and corresponding delineation of anatomical regions of interest.  It also includes the instance segmentation of neurons across all sections, along with extracted neuronal features. Sections were stained by immunohistochemistry using the neural Nuclei (NeuN) antibody staining neurons. The sections were digitized at 20x in bright field (~3-5GB / section) by a virtual scanner, Axioscan.Z1 (Zeiss). An expert in neurobiology has manually segmented the main anatomical brain regions using the Allen Atlas as a reference.
Neuron segmentation maps were computed with a deep learning algorithm specifically designed for neuron segmentation ([Wu et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compbiomed.2022.106180)) and optimized with high-performance computing, allowing the process of these multi-gigabyte images. As a result, approximately 900k neurons were segmented. Fifty neuron characteristics, including localisation and morphological features (area, circularity, etc.), were computed on all neurons and provided in the dataset in a structured text format. 
This dataset supports a range of analyses focused on neuronal populations, including counting, morphological profiling and spatial distribution studies, which are of major interest in both physiological and pathophysiological conditions. Furthermore, it provides a valuable resource for investigating the innovative approach of cell-graph representation of cell populations in entire brain sections to perform multiscale analyses (cell population description, automated anatomical segmentation).

name: An optogenetic probe for the specific manipulation of newly potentiated dendritic spines (v1)
description:
We created a pair of constructs aimed at expressing Channelrhodopsin (ChR) selectively at potentiated synapses. The constructs allow activity-dependent expression of the high-performance ChR isoform ChR-XXM in an activity-dependent fashion at dendritic spines. Moreover, the temporal window for the expression of ChR-XXM can be regulated via a tetON system.
The constructs were validated using patch-clamp recordings and demonstrate the possibility to control neuronal firing by specifically acting on the subset of synapses recruited by structural plasticity.
Once inserted in AAV vectors, these constructs will be distributed and reused by the scientific community for studies on the physiopathology of learning and memory.

name: sIPSCs from juvenile (P21-30) C57Bl6/J male mice from CA1 pyramidal neurons receiving input from PV+ interneurons (v1)
description:
A general procedure to fit individual synaptic events recorded from voltage clamp experiments was tested with various sets of experimental data on GABAergic synapses; gephyrin and gephyrin-dependent pathways were chosen as a suitable example of a kinetic model of synaptic transmission. The data used here are obtained from coronal hippocampal slices (300 μm thick) from juvenile (P21-30) C57B16/J male mice receiving input from parvalbumin positive (PV+) interneurons. The dataset contains 614 individual events recorded from 3 different neurons (expC1-C3). The first column of each txt file contains the time in ms and the other columns contain spontaneous inhibitory synaptic currents (sIPSCs) in pA.
Computational modeling of brain circuits requires the definition of many parameters that are difficult to determine from experimental findings. One way to help interpret these data is to fit them using a particular kinetic model. In [1] we proposed a general procedure to fit individual synaptic events recorded from voltage clamp experiments. Starting from any given model description (mod file) in the NEURON simulation environment, the procedure exploits user-defined constraints, dependencies, and rules for the parameters of the model to fit the time course of individual spontaneous synaptic events that are recorded experimentally. A Python version is available for public use, as a Jupyter Notebook in the Collaboratory Portal of the Human Brain Project. To illustrate the potential application of the procedure, we tested its use with various sets of experimental data on GABAergic synapses; gephyrin and gephyrin-dependent pathways were chosen as a suitable example of a kinetic model of synaptic transmission. For individual spontaneous inhibitory events in hippocampal pyramidal CA1 neurons, we found that gephyrin-dependent subcellular pathways may shape synaptic events at different levels, and can be correlated with cell- or event-specific activity history and/or pathological conditions.
Fitting experimental data against a number of different models is a common way to do this (reviewed in [2]), and can help in the subsequent interpretation of the data. In general, experimental traces are fitted using specific approaches for specific purposes (e.g., [3], [4]). However, to the best of our knowledge, there is no easy, user-friendly, general procedure available for this purpose, especially in computational neuroscience. Our aim was thus to identify the appropriate conceptual structure of a procedure to obtain good, reliable fits of raw experimental traces of spontaneous synaptic events. This is an important step because spontaneous synaptic events have been so far exclusively analyzed using traces obtained by averaging many events. However, as can be easily imagined, each synapse in any given neuron has its own, independent, history of activation. The most likely physiological consequence is that the variables relative to the subcellular processes underlying synaptic transmission are different for each synapse. If a researcher is interested in testing a specific kinetic scheme implemented for specific biochemical pathways, the use of individual events is the most appropriate choice, since this approach would give information on the different combinations of model parameters that are consistent with the observed events. Averaging traces will lose a lot of relevant information.
We therefore present here the implementation of a procedure leading to the development of a unifying optimization method for individual synaptic events. Experimental data, kinetic models of synaptic transmission, and fitting parameters and their dependencies can be user defined/provided or gathered from databases. They can be used to generate optimized groups of parameters able to represent a population of synapses, either for simulation purposes or to study the functional consequences of a particular protein or subcellular synaptic transmission pathway. 
[1] Lupascu CA, Morabito A, Merenda E, et al. A General Procedure to Study Subcellular Models of Transsynaptic Signaling at Inhibitory Synapses. Frontiers in Neuroinformatics. 2016;10:23. doi:10.3389/fninf.2016.00023   
[2] Van Geit W., De Schutter E., Achard P. (2008). Automated neuron model optimization techniques: a review. Biol. Cybern. 99, 241–251. 10.1007/s00422-008-0257-6  
[3] Bekkers J. M. (2003). Convolution of mini distributions for fitting evoked synaptic amplitude histograms. J. Neurosci. Methods. 130, 105–114. 10.1016/j.jneumeth.2003.09.018  
[4] Meisl G., Kirkegaard J. B., Arosio P., Michaels T. C., Vendruscolo M., Dobson C. M., et al. . (2016). Molecular mechanisms of protein aggregation from global fitting of kinetic models. Nat. Protoc. 11, 252–272. 10.1038/nprot.2016.010

description:
This dataset SF.VCo contains the distinct cytoarchitectonic subdivision, the ventral cortical nucleus (VCo), of the superficial amygdaloid group (SF) in the individual, single subject template of the MNI Colin 27 as well as the MNI ICBM 152 2009c nonlinear asymmetric reference space.
